chunks: "A thermal relief is the way a pad connects to a copper plane or pour using a few narrow spokes with an air gap around the rest of the pad, instead of fusing the pad solidly into the copper.
You see it as a little wheel or cross around a through-hole pin on a ground plane. The reason is soldering.
A plane is a huge heat sink, so if the pad is solidly tied to it, the iron or the reflow oven has a hard time getting that pad up to solder temperature.
You end up with cold joints, or the part tombstones because one pad melts first, and reworking it is miserable.
The spokes limit how fast heat can leave the pad, so it heats up like an isolated pad but is still electrically connected.
The cost is that the spokes are a bottleneck: they have higher resistance and lower current capacity than a solid connection, and they add a bit of inductance.

So I use reliefs for ordinary through-hole pins and small pads on pours, and I turn them off for high-current power pads, exposed thermal pads where I want heat to flow out, and anything where inductance matters, like some high-frequency ground connections.
Or I make the spokes wider."
